title: Java 11 floor
issueTitle: webtools-udp 2.0.0 ships Java 23 bytecode but README claims JDK 11+
function: The README promises JDK 11 or newer, but every published WebTools artifact is Java 23 bytecode (class-file major 67) whose Gradle Module Metadata declares `org.gradle.jvm.version: 23`, so a consumer on JDK 11 to 22 fails with `UnsupportedClassVersionError`. This run sets one Java floor of 11 in the included `build-logic` build that every module reads, so the published bytecode, its metadata and the JDK API compiled against all match the README. Unit 2 of #55: a bug fix to bytecode and metadata with no public API, state or wire change, local to the build.

wip.detail: Merged through PR #76 as 3949b52; #47 closed. Every module now compiles to the Java 11 floor and `verifyJavaFloor` guards it in `check`. `webtools-scraping` and `webtools-browser` are at 1.0.0a and `webtools-udp` stays at 2.0.0a, none published; the README's install block names the versions on Maven Central. The as-built record and the impact were reconciled after the landing (PR #78). Unit 3 of #55, #62, is no longer blocked by this issue.

gap.summary: No build file sets `jvmTarget`, `-Xjdk-release`, a Java `release` or a toolchain, so class files and `org.gradle.jvm.version` follow the JDK that runs the build: every published artifact is Java 23 bytecode (major 67) declaring 23. The multiplatform plugin writes the build JDK's version into its attribute.
gap.detail: `jvmTarget` alone lowers the class-file version but not the API surface: on a JDK 23 host, `MutableList.removeFirst()` compiled to JDK 21's `List.removeFirst` with no warning.
evidence: build-logic/src/main/kotlin/webtools.kotlin-jvm-library.gradle.kts:6-7 — no `jvmTarget` or toolchain; output follows the build JDK until #47
research/java-11-floor.md F1, F5 — what each setting does; the existing sources compile under `-Xjdk-release=11` with zero errors

asBuilt.summary: Built as decided: `WebToolsBuild.JAVA_FLOOR = 11` drives `jvmTarget`, `-Xjdk-release` and the Java compatibility settings of the Kotlin/JVM plugin and the `jvm()` options and `TargetJvmVersion` attribute of the multiplatform plugin; the ASM pin is gone. The three modules' jars hold 98, 4 and 2 classes, all class-file major 55, with no compiler warning.
asBuilt.verified: Procedures A to E, recorded after landing: the three modules compile under the floor with no warning and the guard passes on each; against a `36fd879` build every class went from major 67 to 55 with `javap -protected` identical; every class loads on a real JDK 11 (98, 4 and 2, none failing; the baseline jars load none); `build-logic`'s suites pass on JDK 17 and JDK 23.

options.name: `WebToolsBuild.JAVA_FLOOR = 11` driving `jvmTarget`, `-Xjdk-release` and the Java compatibility settings (Kotlin/JVM plugin) and the `TargetJvmVersion` attribute (multiplatform plugin), on the JDK that runs the build
options.why: `-Xjdk-release` limits the API to Java 11, which `jvmTarget` alone does not, and it needs no JDK 11 on the build host. A `jvmToolchain(11)` would need #58's resolver bump, make every consumer's composite build need a JDK 11, and still write no multiplatform attribute.

options.name: `jvmTarget = 11` alone
options.why: It lowers the class-file version but not the API surface: on a JDK 23 host `MutableList.removeFirst()` compiled to JDK 21's `List.removeFirst` without a warning.
options.source: ../research/README.md § Build, publishing and the Java 11 floor

options.name: `jvmToolchain(11)` as the floor
options.why: It gives the same API limit at the cost of the foojay resolver bump and a JDK 11 on every consumer's composite machine, and it still writes no multiplatform attribute.
options.wins: If the level tests had to run on a JDK 11 inside this work.

verdict.summary: Add `JAVA_FLOOR = 11` to `WebToolsBuild` and set `jvmTarget`, `-Xjdk-release` and `java { sourceCompatibility; targetCompatibility }` from it in the Kotlin/JVM plugin, and the `jvm()` compiler options and the `TargetJvmVersion` attribute in the multiplatform plugin. The ASM pin, which existed only because class files followed the build JDK, is removed.
verdict.defense: A bug fix local to the build: the bytecode, the metadata and the API compiled against change, while no source file, no public signature (`javap -protected` identical) and no POM beyond two versions moves. One constant keeps the flag and `jvmTarget` paired, as Kotlin requires.

options.name: A `verifyJavaFloor` task in `check` that scans the built jars, the generated `.module` files and the resolved runtime classpath
options.why: It reads the files a consumer receives rather than the settings that should produce them, and it fails when there is nothing to check, so a wiring mistake cannot pass silently. The classpath scan catches a Java 17 dependency that publishes no Gradle metadata.

options.name: The floor's checks as a level test
options.why: The facts live in the publishable files, the built jars and the generated `.module` files, so the guard is a Gradle verification task wired into `check`, not a level test.

verdict.summary: Both plugins register `verifyJavaFloor` as a dependency of `check`; it fails on a class above major 55 outside `META-INF/versions/`, a library variant declaring another `org.gradle.jvm.version`, or nothing to check. The regression test of record, `PublishedJvmVersionAttributeIntegrationTest`, expects 11 instead of the test JVM's version and fails today.
verdict.defense: Nothing that reads the produced bytes exists today, so the defect could not fail a build. The guard is configuration-cache compatible and up to date when its inputs are unchanged.

impact.summary: A fix to the published bytes, built as planned: every module's class files are Java 11 bytecode built against the Java 11 API, and its Gradle Module Metadata declares `org.gradle.jvm.version: 11` instead of 23; every class loads on a real JDK 11, so consumers on JDK 11 to 22 can use it once released. No source, public API or wire format changed. The fix rides in `webtools-udp` 2.0.0a and `webtools-scraping` / `webtools-browser` 1.0.0a, none of them published yet.

release.note: trailing letters; `webtools-udp` keeps its unreleased version; nothing was tagged or published, and the README's install block names the versions on Maven Central until the lettered ones are released

downstream.summary: The released Java 23 builds fail to load with `UnsupportedClassVersionError`; the lettered versions load once published. Consumers on JDK 23 or newer see no difference.

Class files went from major 67 to 55 (98, 4 and 2 classes) and the metadata's JVM version from 23 to 11 on the API and runtime variants. Measured against `36fd879`: `javap -protected` is identical for every class, `webtools-udp`'s POM is identical and the two legacy POMs differ only in `<version>`.

They inherit a multiplatform plugin that compiles their `jvm()` target at the floor, sets the attribute, runs `verifyJavaFloor` in `check` and carries no ASM pin; Gradle rejects any dependency declaring a higher JVM.

A module's `check` also builds its sources and javadoc jars and metadata and runs the guard, about a second for the largest module; `./gradlew verifyJavaFloor` runs the guard alone. Building still needs a JDK 17 to 26.
On JDK 21, it was not blocked and needs nothing.

adaptation.summary: Move to the lettered versions once they are published, requesting them `strictly` where the graph also asks for the plain release.

Set no `jvmTarget`, toolchain, flag or `TargetJvmVersion` of their own, declare no second JVM-based target, call no JDK API newer than 11 and use no `@JvmRecord`; `test-support`'s fixtures variants set the attribute from `WebToolsBuild.JAVA_FLOOR` and add their jar to the guard.

api.summary: Surface of the included `build-logic` build, internal to the repository and not published; the later units' build scripts read `JAVA_FLOOR`. No published library API changes.

conversion.what: On JDK 11 to 22, move to `webtools-udp` 2.0.0a or `webtools-scraping` / `webtools-browser` 1.0.0a once they are published.
Where the dependency graph also asks for the plain release, request the lettered version `strictly`.
